name: Vedapuriswarar Temple, Thiruvedhikudi
deity: Shiva as Vedapuriswarar (Vazhaimadunathar), with the goddess Mangayarkarasi
period: Fourth shrine of the Saptha Sthanam of Thiruvaiyaru; Chola stonework of the 9th century, sung in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Chola, with gopurams added up to the Thanjavur Nayak period
summary: At Thiruvedhikudi, Shiva is the lord of the Vedas, attended by a Ganesha who tilts his head to listen to their chant; the village is said to have sent the Vedic priests for Nandi's wedding.

sections.history: Thiruvedhikudi is a small village south of the Kaveri, a few kilometres from Thiruvaiyaru, whose very name ties it to the Vedas. Appar and Sambandar sang of its lord, and the temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Tevaram. The oldest masonry of the present shrine dates from the Chola period of the ninth century, and gopurams and outer structures were added over the following centuries, up to the time of the Thanjavur Nayaks. The temple is cared for today by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of Tamil Nadu.
sections.architecture: The Vedas are written into the building itself. Four Nandis are placed on the outer wall and on the vimana over the sanctum, one facing each of the four directions, and they are read as the four Vedas keeping watch over the lord. In the maha mandapam sits Veda Vinayakar, a Ganesha whose head is tilted to one side as though listening to Vedic recitation. The goddess Mangayarkarasi has a separate shrine in the outer courtyard, approached through a Vasantha mandapam.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that Brahma, Surya and Kubera each worshipped the lord here and were blessed, and the village is remembered as a place of Brahma's worship. The temple story also links it with the Vedas restored to the world after Vishnu, taking the horse-headed form of Hayagriva, recovered them from the demon who had carried them off beneath the ocean. The lord's other name, Vazhaimadunathar, is tied in local tradition to a sacred pool and the banana plant.
sections.festivals: In the Saptha Sthanam festival of Chithirai (April–May), the procession reaches Thiruvedhikudi after Thiruchotruthurai. Tradition holds that the village, true to its name, sent the Vedic priests who chanted at Nandi's wedding. The temple is also regarded as a place to pray for a good marriage. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Pause in the maha mandapam before Veda Vinayakar and notice the tilt of his head, then walk around the sanctum to find the Nandis facing the four quarters. Families come here to pray for an auspicious marriage, often going on to the goddess Mangayarkarasi in her own shrine. The village is quiet, and the temple combines well with Thiruchotruthurai and Thirukandiyur.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvedhikudi lies on the southern side of the Kaveri, about 7 km by road from Thiruvaiyaru and roughly 10 km north of Thanjavur; local buses, autos and taxis serve it from both towns. Thanjavur is the nearest major railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport, about 60 km away, is the nearest airport.
